slides.title: Four things to start with.
slides.text: Create, read, update and delete are {operations}: things you can do with data. A rule gives a {role}, a set of identities, some operations on one piece of data. Never a person directly, always a role. The owner writes the first rules; later we'll see how a role can be allowed to pass its own on.
slides.deep: A rule is a signed certificate: role, data, list of operations, conditions, expiry, plus the proof chain back to the seal. Rules are written only by the owner (D30). Conditions come later in this chapter, proofs in Checking, expiry in Endings.

slides.title: You share the list with Mia.
slides.text: You make a role “home”, give it read, create and update on the list, and add Mia. She can see the list, add things and tick them off. She can't delete it, and she can't change the rules.
slides.deep: Mia's identity is added to the role “home”. Technically: the owner signs a membership change and wraps the role key for Mia's identity key (both explained in the Keys chapter). The data's rules don't change at all.

slides.title: The plumber gets one item.
slides.text: “Fix the tap” is its own little piece of data, linked from the list. Born inside the list, it starts with the list's rules. You add one more: the role “plumber” may read and update this item, and nothing else.
slides.deep: Read access can only be as fine as a key. So an item shared on its own is its own piece of data, with its own data key, linked from the list. New data born inside the list copies the list's rules once, at birth.

slides.title: Every rule is one sentence.
slides.text: A rule says: this role may perform these operations, on this data, until a date: its {expiry}. Nothing more. Everything anyone may ever do with your data is written in rules like this one.
slides.deep: A rule is a signed certificate with one shape everywhere: who (a role), on what (this data), operations (each optionally narrowed by at, where or a limit), expiry, and a proof chain back to the seal. An identity's own rules use the same shape (Identity chapter). People see “rule”; underneath it is a capability.

slides.title: What a rule can allow.
slides.text: Each operation is one thing a role may do. Some are about the content, and one, {share}, passes a narrower copy of a rule on. Want, keep and sync are about carrying data; they come in the Carriers chapter.
list: Passing on: share, giving other roles a narrower copy, which you can end again.
Operations that only look at data, like searching, need only read.
Writing rules is not on the list: only the owner does that.
slides.deep: The full list of operations: create, read, update, delete, share, want, keep, sync. Writing rules is not an operation anyone can be given; it belongs to the owner (D30). Engine operations that only read need read.

slides.title: Conditions make a rule narrower.
slides.text: Each operation can carry {conditions}: only this part of the data, only entries that match, only so many times.
slides.deep: Conditions are evaluated by every verifying peer: at (a path prefix), where (matching entries, for example author = $self), limits. Like Meadowcap's areas, each condition can only narrow.

slides.title: Passing a rule on only narrows it.
slides.text: If home's rule allows share, Mia can give other roles a narrower copy: “grandma's” may read, the plumber may read and update one item. She can end what she gave, but no one else's. And if her own rule ends, everything she passed on ends with it. Only the owner's rules never fall this way.
slides.deep: Attenuation: each appended block can only remove operations, shorten the expiry or add conditions; a verifier intersects all blocks. A delegate may end only rules it issued. When a rule ends, every rule issued under it ends too (cascade); the owner's rules are the root. Writes by a removed delegate that never saw the ending are dropped.

slides.title: Only the owner never expires.
slides.text: The rule the seal signed at birth names the owner. It has no expiry, so data can never end up with nobody allowed to look after it. Only the owner can hand it over to another identity. Every other rule expires.
slides.deep: The genesis certificate has no expiry. Ownership moves only through a hand-over signed by the owner under its own rules.

slides.title: Rules, in short.
list: A rule: this role may perform these operations, on this data, until then.
The owner writes the first rules; roles with share pass narrower copies on.
Conditions narrow a rule; nothing can widen it.
slides.deep: Rules are capabilities attached to roles, granted only by the owner, narrowable, expiring by default, ended by events, and checked offline by every peer.
